pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📐 **Strand 3 — Geometry And Measurement**
Shape, space, measurement, position and movement — the mathematics of the world around us.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B9.3.3)
- B9.3.3.1 — Demonstrate understanding of how to perform an enlargement on a geometrical shape given a scale factor and describe the properties of the image under the transformation (i.e. congruence, similarity, etc.).

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- recognise enlargement in everyday life
- enlarge shapes about a centre with positive, negative and fractional scale factors
- find the centre and scale factor of an enlargement from an object and its image
- verify that enlargement produces similar shapes, and congruent shapes only when k = ±1

pages.title: Enlargement in everyday life
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Know examples of situations in everyday life that depict enlargement.
Curriculum indicator B9.3.3.1.1
An **enlargement** changes the size of a shape but keeps its shape. Everyday examples: a projector throwing a picture onto a screen; enlarging or reducing a photograph on a phone; a photocopier set to 150% or 50%; maps and scale drawings; a magnifying glass; shadows of objects in torchlight; models of cars and buildings.
[[fig:m9-f31|Figure 12.1: A projector enlarges a slide about the lamp (centre of enlargement)]]

pages.title: Drawing enlargements
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Understand enlargement and identify real-life situations involving enlargement; draw enlargements of shapes using a given scale factor.
Curriculum indicator B9.3.3.1.2
> 🔑 **Key idea: Enlargement** — An enlargement with **centre O** and **scale factor k** maps every point P to P′ on the line OP such that **OP′ = k × OP**. If O is the origin, (x, y) → (kx, ky). Every length in the image is k times the corresponding length in the object; angles are unchanged.
## ✏️ Example 12.1
Triangle P has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1) and (1, 2). a) Enlarge P with centre O(0, 0) and scale factor 2 to get Q. b) Enlarge P with centre O and scale factor −1 to get R. c) State the single transformation mapping P onto Q, and P onto R.
**Solution**
a) Multiply each coordinate by 2: Q has vertices **(2, 2), (6, 2), (2, 4)**.
b) Multiply each coordinate by −1: R has vertices **(−1, −1), (−3, −1), (−1, −2)**.
[[fig:m9-f32]]
Figure 12.2: Enlargements of triangle P with centre O
c) P → Q: **an enlargement, centre O(0, 0), scale factor 2**. P → R: **an enlargement, centre O, scale factor −1** (the same as a rotation of 180° about O).
> 🔑 **Key idea: Effects of the scale factor k** — **k > 1**: the image is larger, on the same side of the centre. **0 < k < 1**: the image is smaller (a **reduction**). **k = 1**: the image is identical in the same place. **k < 0** (negative): the image is on the **opposite** side of the centre and **upside down**; if k < −1 it is larger, if −1 < k < 0 it is smaller. **k = −1**: the image is congruent (a half-turn).

pages.title: Example 12.2
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 12.2
Enlarge the square with vertices (2, 2), (6, 2), (6, 6), (2, 6) with centre (0, 0) and scale factor [[1/2]].
**Solution**
(x, y) → ([[1/2]]x, [[1/2]]y): **(1, 1), (3, 1), (3, 3), (1, 3)**. The image is a square of side 2 — a reduction.
## ✏️ Example 12.3
Using an object and its image, determine the scale factor and centre: triangle ABC with A(2, 1), B(4, 1), C(2, 2) is mapped onto A′(2, 1), B′(8, 1), C′(2, 4).
**Solution**
Lengths: AB = 2, A′B′ = 6, so **k = 3**. Join B to B′ and C to C′ and extend: the lines meet at **A(2, 1)**, which maps to itself. Centre = **(2, 1)**. Check: C is 1 unit above the centre; C′ is 3 units above ✓.

pages.body:

pages.title: Similarity and congruence under enlargement
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Investigate the concept of congruent and similar shapes.
Curriculum indicator B9.3.3.1.3
| **Property** | **Enlargement (k ≠ ±1)** | **Enlargement (k = ±1)** |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Angles | unchanged | unchanged |  |  |
| Lengths | multiplied by | k |  | unchanged |
| Area | multiplied by k² | unchanged |  |  |
| Object and image are … | **similar** | **congruent** |  |  |
## ✏️ Example 12.4
Use Example 12.1 to verify that triangles P and Q are similar but not congruent, and that P and R are congruent.
**Solution**
P: sides 2, 1 and √5; Q: sides 4, 2 and 2√5 — each is twice as long, and the right angle and other angles are the same. So **P and Q are similar** (not congruent). R has sides 2, 1 and √5 — the same as P — so **P and R are congruent**. Area of P = 1, area of Q = 4 = 2² × 1 ✓.

pages.title: Exercise 12.3
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 12.3** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. A photograph 10 cm by 15 cm is enlarged so that the shorter side is 25 cm. Find the longer side and the scale factor. Are the photographs similar?
2. A triangle of area 12 cm² is enlarged with scale factor 3. What is the area of the image?
3. Which transformations always give congruent images? Which can give similar but not congruent images?

questions.q: A photograph 10 cm by 15 cm is enlarged so that the shorter side is 25 cm. Find the longer side and the scale factor. Are the photographs similar?
A triangle of area 12 cm² is enlarged with scale factor 3. What is the area of the image?
Which transformations always give congruent images? Which can give similar but not congruent images?

parts.a: Reflection, translation and rotation (and enlargement with k = ±1) give congruent images; enlargement with k ≠ ±1 gives similar images.

pages.title: Chapter 12 summary
pages.body:
- Enlargement: centre O, scale factor k; OP′ = k × OP; about the origin (x, y) → (kx, ky).
- |k| > 1 enlarges, |k| < 1 reduces; negative k puts the image on the other side, inverted.
- Images are similar (equal angles, proportional sides); congruent only when k = ±1. Area scales by k².
